## In brief - Upward revision of Swiss GDP for 2026 to 1.7% - Estimate for 2027 unchanged at 1.6% - Unemployment forecast at 3.1% in 2026 and 3.0% in 2027 ## Key facts - Press release date: September 17, 2026 - 2026 GDP growth: 1.7% - 2027 GDP growth: 1.6% - 2nd quarter 2026 growth: 1.5% - Expected average inflation: 0.6% - 2026 unemployment rate: 3.1% - 2027 unemployment rate: 3.0%
The Confederation's expert group for economic forecasts published an update of its economic estimates for Switzerland in Bern on September 17, 2026. According to the report finalized on September 8, 2026, the Swiss economy is showing a recovery phase with an upward revision of gross domestic product growth for the current year. Growth of 1.7% is now expected for the current year, a figure significantly higher than the previous June forecast which indicated 0.9%. For 2027, however, the estimate remains unchanged at 1.6% net of sporting events. Swiss GDP recently recorded a strong increase, driven in the second quarter of 2026 by an extraordinary momentum equal to 1.5%.
### Sectoral dynamics of GDP The growth recorded in the second quarter of 2026 was broadly supported both at the sectoral level and from the demand side, although experts warn that this may be an overestimate of the underlying economic momentum. Indeed, almost half of this growth is attributable to the added value of the chemical and pharmaceutical industry, a sector historically characterized by strong fluctuations, accompanied by a marked increase in exports. In light of these factors, the Confederation's experts expect a reversal of the trend for the second half of the year. Despite this, the economic situation remains essentially on a recovery path and the excellent performance of the first half justifies the positive revision for the whole of 2026. Foreign trade is expected to contribute to a greater extent than June forecasts, supported by the positive economic trend so far, the slightly better global economic context and the recent depreciation of the Swiss franc, which facilitates export sectors particularly exposed to exchange rate fluctuations. Domestic demand instead continues with a moderate progression, while the greater exploitation of productive capacities favors investment activities and private consumption continues to grow in a controlled manner. The forecasts drawn up by the group of experts outline an overall stable economic scenario for the Swiss labour market, with direct repercussions on employment and price stability. The favourable economic trend is reflected in a gradual decrease in the unemployment rate, expected at 3.1% in the annual average for 2026 and forecast to fall further to 3.0% for 2027, confirming previous estimates without significant changes. On the inflation front, despite recent increases, prices remained at moderate levels until recently. Futures markets also indicate a possible drop in oil prices in the coming months, leading experts to confirm an average annual inflation rate of 0.6% for both 2026 and 2027.
### Growth scenarios and international recovery A further recovery in global demand is expected for 2027, driven mainly by European countries and first and foremost by Germany, whose exit from the phase of weakness in recent years will offer decisive support to the Swiss economy. GDP, adjusted for sporting events, is expected to grow by 1.6%. However, significant cyclical risks remain linked to international geopolitical and commercial factors. The conflict in the Middle East represents an element of strong uncertainty for the global economy: if the price of oil were to remain at high levels, it could weigh heavily on energy costs and push inflation upwards even in Switzerland. Given the very low inventories in Europe, further price increases cannot be ruled out even for natural gas. Added to this are uncertainties regarding trade policy and US import tariffs, which for now are assumed to remain at current levels but remain subject to possible future adjustments, including developments linked to the investigation launched on March 11, 2026 by the United States into alleged overcapacity in the industrial production of several States, including Switzerland. Any corrections on the financial markets and the increase in global financing costs could exert additional upward pressure on the Swiss franc.

The forecasts on Swiss economic growth for the current year show an exceptionally strong upward revision, fueled by the favorable cyclical trend recorded in the second quarter. This was communicated by the State Secretariat for Economic Affairs (SECO), whose officials emphasize that the national economy is poised to gain new momentum. Specifically, the head of SECO's Economic Policy Directorate, Roland Indergand, highlighted the magnitude of the revision compared to previous estimates. According to the updated data released by the federal agency, Switzerland's gross domestic product (GDP) should record an increase of 1.7% for the current year. This figure marks a clear improvement over the 0.9% that had been hypothesized in June. Regarding the medium term, the forecast of +1.6% already formulated for 2027 is instead confirmed in full. The positive trend of the Swiss economy finds confirmation in the dynamics of productive sectors and exchanges with foreign markets, offering an overall more solid macroeconomic picture for residents, businesses, and economic operators active on the national territory. This upward revision fits into a global context in evolution, where the Swiss industrial fabric's capacity to react continues to represent the main engine of national and cantonal economic development. ### The engine of foreign trade At the basis of this economic acceleration lies mainly the contribution of foreign trade, whose performance exceeds the estimates formulated in June. This positive result is supported by a slightly better world economic context and by the effects related to the weakening of the franc on international currency markets. If in recent months the forecasts indicated even a contraction of exports by 0.7%, the current scenario outlined by SECO overturns expectations, speaking of an actual growth of 1.5% for Swiss exported goods. In parallel, federal authorities register a moderate progression of domestic demand within the country. The progressive and greater utilization of production capacities by companies will translate into a positive impulse for private and corporate investment activities. At the same time, private consumption in Switzerland should continue along a trajectory of moderate increase, ensuring stability of domestic spending and supporting retail trade and services in the various Swiss cantons. L'evoluzione positiva della congiuntura economica nazionale si ripercuote in modo diretto anche sulle dinamiche del mercato del lavoro svizzero. Secondo le analisi e le proiezioni elaborate dalla SECO, il consolidamento della crescita economica determinerà una graduale ma costante diminuzione del tasso di disoccupazione su scala nazionale. In base alle stime ufficiali pubblicate, la disoccupazione dovrebbe attestarsi su una media annua del 3,1% per quanto riguarda il 2026. Per l'anno successivo, ovvero il 2027, le previsioni indicano un ulteriore calo, con il tasso destinato a scendere leggermente fino a raggiungere la soglia del 3,0%. Questa prospettiva di stabilizzazione e rafforzamento dell'occupazione offre un quadro rassicurante per la forza lavoro residente e per quanti operano nel mercato del lavoro elvetico, riducendo le tensioni occupazionali registrate in precedenti fasi di incertezza macroeconomica globale. Sul versante dell'andamento dei prezzi e del potere d'acquisto, i mercati a termine lasciano intravedere segnali favorevoli nei prossimi mesi, guidati in particolare da un atteso calo del corso del petrolio. ## In brief - Heavy defeat for the neutrality initiative - Second SSR poll published in September - 63% of the electorate expects to vote no - Decline in support also for the food initiative
## Key facts - Voting date: September 27, 2026 - gfs.bern poll period: September 2-9, 2026 - Interviewed sample: 12,916 voters - Margin of error: +/-2.8 percentage points - Support for neutrality initiative: 34% - Opponents of neutrality initiative: 63% - Undecided on neutrality initiative: 3% - Support for food initiative: 33% - Opponents of food initiative: 64% - Undecided on food initiative: 3%
About ten days before the federal votes on September 27, 2026, the neutrality initiative is in a difficult position and heading towards a ballot defeat. According to the second poll by the Swiss Broadcasting Corporation (SSR), conducted by the gfs.bern research institute between September 2 and 9 among a sample of 12,916 voters with a margin of error between +/-2.8 percentage points, 63% of the electorate plans to reject the text launched by Pro Switzerland. Only 34% support the proposal and 3% remain undecided, while the no front has lost nine percentage points in a month.
### Support dynamics and political orientation The advance of the no vote is observed homogeneously throughout the federal territory. Even within the Swiss People's Party (SVP), which is the only party supporting the initiative, approval of the text has dropped by nine percentage points in a month, standing at 77%. gfs.bern political scientist Lukas Golder observes that the issue is more open than expected within the centrist electorate, as it is not one of the party's preferred topics, unlike migration or relations with the European Union where the base lines up more solidly. Voters of all other parties plan to reject the text increasingly clearly, while people without party affiliation have moved into the no camp, leaving in favor only those who harbor distrust towards the government, albeit with scarce support.
### Geographic and territorial evolution The gap between city and countryside, which had clearly emerged in the first poll, has progressively narrowed over the weeks preceding the popular consultation on September 27, 2026. By now, the initiative calling for the inclusion of a restrictive conception of neutrality in the Constitution is widely rejected even in the rural areas of Switzerland. From an argumentative standpoint, those who oppose perpetual neutrality anchored in the Constitution hold a clear advantage, since more than two-thirds of the respondents fear that the text could harm the country's security, limiting Switzerland's ability to cooperate with other states in this specific area. The definitive projection by gfs.bern political scientists clearly indicates that a rejection of the initiative represents the most likely scenario for this round of voting. ## Analysis of voting dynamics and comparison with the food initiative
The federal votes of September 27, 2026 present a complex picture involving multiple items submitted to a popular vote. Alongside the debate on Swiss neutrality, which aims to enshrine a stricter and more restrictive conception in the Constitution, the electorate's attention is also polarized on the initiative asking the Confederation to promote the production and consumption of plant-based foods. This second text has also seen a drastic decrease in support compared to the previous survey conducted by the gfs.bern institute on behalf of SSR.
### The text on plant-based food While in mid-August the supporting and opposing camps were still neck and neck in the public debate, almost two-thirds of the people interviewed, equal to 64%, now intend to vote no ahead of the September 27, 2026 deadline. Only 33% support the plant-based food initiative, while the share of undecided voters stands at 3%. This drastic trend reversal highlights how the information campaign and political debate have eroded initial consensus, shifting the absolute majority of voters toward the rejection of the federal regulatory proposal.
### Behavior of the diaspora and political parties An element of particular interest emerging from the second poll concerns the Fifth Switzerland, namely Swiss citizens residing abroad. A month ago the diaspora was in favor of the food initiative, but currently opposes it by a large majority with 59% against. Nonetheless, the text maintains higher support within this specific electorate, where 37% declared their intention to vote yes and 4% remain undecided. Experts explain this phenomenon by recalling that the diaspora historically tends to vote more in favor of ecological issues and is simultaneously less involved in national debates focused on the technical shortcomings of the text. Regarding Swiss political forces, the Greens electorate represents the only exception in the party landscape, continuing to support the food initiative with a percentage of 78%. Conversely, sympathizers of the Social Democratic Party (SP) and the Green Liberal Party (GLP), who at the beginning of the campaign showed significant openness, have changed their voting orientation over the weeks.

## In brief - Growth of cyber insurance in Switzerland in 2025 - Insured companies rose to 72,000, a 7% increase compared to the previous year - Strong growth among private individuals: +18% to 480,000 insured
## Key facts - Association: Swiss Insurance Association (SIA) - Reference year: 2025 - Insured companies: 72,000 - Company growth: 7% - Insured private individuals: 480,000 - Private growth: 18% - Private premiums: 29 million CHF - Business premiums: 153 million CHF - Insured Swiss companies: approximately 11% - Future event: Cyber Insurance Summit 2026 in Bern on November 5th
Cyber insurance, meaning insurance products that protect individuals and businesses from damages caused by cyberattacks or digital system issues, is experiencing a marked growth phase in the Swiss economic landscape. According to data released by the Swiss Insurance Association (SIA) as part of its annual sector survey, in 2025 the number of insured companies rose to 72,000, marking a 7% increase compared to the previous year. Even more sustained is the progression recorded among private clients, where the percentage growth reaches 18%, bringing the total to 480,000 active policies. From a financial volume perspective, the SIA survey highlights that collected premiums reached 29 million CHF for private clients, while the business sector generated a volume of 153 million CHF. This dynamic allows the sector to firmly establish itself among the fastest-growing within the Swiss insurance coverage market, responding to a demand for protection that evolves in parallel with the digitalization of commercial processes and daily life.
### The situation of companies and SMEs in the Swiss market
Despite the general increase in volumes and subscriptions, significant structural differences remain among the various types of businesses operating nationally. SIA findings reveal that only about 11% of Swiss companies are currently covered by insurance against cyber risks. Analyzing the distribution of this data, it clearly emerges that the greatest gaps are particularly concentrated among small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), which show lower adoption rates compared to large structures. Conversely, well over half of large companies already have specific coverage to handle any digital incidents or system blocks. This disproportion highlights how the widespread economic fabric, consisting predominantly of smaller entities, has not yet fully bridged the protection gap despite the growing exposure to cyber threats that characterizes the current Swiss economic context. The in-depth analysis conducted by the Swiss Insurance Association highlights that the cyber risk coverage sector plays a strategic role not only in safeguarding company balance sheets following an attack, but also in improving overall operational security. Swiss SMEs, while representing the segment with the greatest coverage gaps, are paradoxically those that could derive the greatest benefits from the assistance services associated with these policies. In addition to direct financial compensation for damages suffered following a cyber incident, insurance contracts regularly include targeted preventive services and the possibility of rapidly activating the support of experts specialized in digital emergency management. Heidi Fröhlich, head of non-life and reinsurance at the SIA, emphasizes that cyber insurance contributes significantly to strengthening the cyber resilience of companies, acting as a fundamental pillar in corporate risk management.
### The impact of cyber risks and upcoming institutional appointments
Cyber attacks currently constitute one of the most significant dangers to the business continuity of Swiss companies, surpassing many traditional threats in complexity and frequency. To address this evolution of risk and encourage dialogue between industry operators, institutions, and businesses, the sector's agenda includes targeted in-depth sessions. Among these, the Cyber Insurance Summit 2026 stands out, an important symposium entirely dedicated to the topic of digital protection and insurance coverage, scheduled for next November 5 in the city of Bern. In a context characterized by a sharp increase in the population in Switzerland, there is currently a marked shortage of housing which, however, could soon diminish in some regions of the country. This is what emerges from a study published by the real estate consulting firm Wüest Partner, according to which the lowest point in housing construction should be overcome in the coming years. The research offers a detailed overview of the future prospects of the Swiss real estate market, outlining a recovery in residential building production after years of contraction.
## # Estimates and comparison with previous years Analyzing the data provided by the Federal Statistical Office (FSO), in 2024 the net increase in housing in Switzerland was just 40,000 units. The situation registered a further slowdown for the current year, with an estimate made by Wüest Partner indicating an increase of only 39,000 housing units for 2025, marking the lowest level recorded since 2009 to date. The foundations that have made this future recovery of the Swiss construction and real estate sector possible were laid several years ago. According to the analysis released by Wüest Partner, the development process began in 2020, a year in which the number of vacant dwellings, after increasing for a long period, began to decline rapidly. At the same time, there was a net growth in the market value of residential properties. These specific market conditions generated strong economic incentives for the construction of new housing projects, simultaneously stimulating further development initiatives nationwide. ### Slowdown factors and project timelines Despite the initial impetus generated in 2020, several years usually pass from the time a construction project is conceived to the actual delivery of the finished home. The main reasons for this timeline include greater complexity in the planning and construction of new housing, caused by the introduction of additional building regulations, as well as rising construction costs and interest rate trends. These factors acted temporarily as a brake on the sector. In the meantime, however, many of the projects initiated and developed since 2020 have overcome the complex preliminary phases and are now close to completion, paving the way for the increase in deliveries expected for the 2026-2027 period and helping to give new breath to the market.

More than three hours of debate this morning in the Council of States were not enough to finish examining the government project aimed at strengthening systemic banks, particularly UBS, in case of difficulties. The debate will continue next Wednesday with the position of the finance minister, Karin Keller-Sutter. The Federal Council hopes that systemic banks will fully cover their foreign subsidiaries with own capital, in order to avoid a repeat of a crisis similar to that of Credit Suisse in 2023. This measure should entail an estimated outlay of 20 billion francs for UBS.
### The position of the preparatory committee
The preparatory committee judged the government's solution too burdensome for UBS, considering that it could prejudice the institute's competitiveness internationally. For this reason a compromise solution was presented that envisages coverage of foreign subsidiaries for 50% with first-class core capital CET1 and for 50% with AT1 Additional Tier 1 bonds. Currently the regulation provides for a rule of 45% core capital combined with 17% in AT1 bonds. AT1 bonds are high-yield securities convertible into own capital or written down in case of serious financial difficulties, as happened in the case of Credit Suisse, a situation that has generated a legal dispute still pending before the Federal Tribunal. According to the committee's proposal, such bonds should contribute significantly to financial stabilization already in an early phase of the crisis.
During the opening debate, the compromise proposal was strongly contested by several political parties, in particular by the left and the Centre. The main fear is that the measure would be insufficient to address a large-scale financial crisis, leaving open the risk that taxpayers and the State would have to intervene to rescue the banks, as already happened in the past both for UBS and for Credit Suisse. Among the supporters of the compromise are various parliamentarians who highlight the need to balance the stability of the financial centre with the global competitiveness of the bank, avoiding negative repercussions on the real economy and on access to credit for Swiss businesses and families. ## A balance between stability and competitiveness
During today's session in the chamber, several speakers advocated for the solution put forward by the parliamentary commission. Tiana Moser of the Zurich Socialist Party described the measure as a balanced tightening and a typical Swiss compromise, stressing that the financial centre must certainly increase its resilience to crises, but that at the same time a major bank must be able to maintain its competitiveness on international markets. Similar considerations were expressed by Ticino centre senator Fabio Regazzi, who acted both as a representative of Ticino and as president of the Swiss Union of Arts and Trades USAM. For the Locarno entrepreneur, an excessive regulatory tightening such as that desired by the Federal Council risks weighing excessively on the financial centre, with the concrete danger that UBS would pass these costs on to local companies that need financing and credit on sustainable terms, as well as to households.
### Economic impact on Ticino Canton and the sector
Fabio Regazzi highlighted that the insurance and banking sector contributes 7% of Ticino's GDP and generates over 10% of the taxes paid to the canton of Ticino. For this reason, according to the senator, it is indispensable to adopt a balanced regulatory framework that favours the bank's resilience without penalising its commercial competitiveness. Along the same line, councillor Thierry Burkart of the PLR argues that, applying the commission's solution, UBS should constitute an additional 13 billion francs of AT1 capital. The proposal of the parliamentary majority aligns with international realities, and the use of AT1 instruments represents a widely tested and well‑known tool for sector operators. Moreover, many speakers have stressed that the government's proposal is punitive towards UBS, as it does not adequately recognise the role played by the institution in 2023 when, by acquiring Credit Suisse, it avoided a systemic crisis on global financial markets.
### Position of the parliamentary minority
Of opposite view is the strong minority led by Peter Hegglin, which maintains that foreign holdings must be covered by 90% of top‑tier core capital. This demand is directly based on the shortcomings and lessons learned during the Credit Suisse crisis. According to the proponents of this stricter line, a high proportion of primary capital would send an unequivocal signal of stability, security and reliability of the entire Swiss financial centre, drastically reducing the likelihood of future public bail‑out interventions at the expense of the national community.

With the continuation of work scheduled for next week and the expected intervention of Finance Minister Karin Keller-Swiss, Parliament is called upon to resolve the issues concerning the ratio between primary own funds and convertible debt instruments such as AT1 bonds. item.title: SMI: Galderma and Sandoz enter, Kühne+Nagel and Swisscom exit
item.description: Big news for the Swiss stock index SMI established by SIX: Galderma and Sandoz enter, while Kühne+Nagel and Swisscom come out. The health sector rises to 40%.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Galderma and Sandoz join the SMI - Kühne+Nagel and Swisscom leave - Update established by SIX - The healthcare sector rises to 40%
## Key facts - Entry date: From Monday - Stock index: Swiss Market Index (SMI) - Incoming companies: Galderma and Sandoz - Outgoing companies: Kühne+Nagel and Swisscom - Stock exchange operator: SIX - Main criteria: Average trading volume and free-float capitalization - New weight of the healthcare sector: 40% - Previous healthcare weight: 36%
### The revision of the Swiss stock index Starting Monday, the Swiss Market Index (SMI), the most important Swiss stock index, is changing its face with the entry of skin care product manufacturer Galderma and generic drug maker Sandoz. To make room for the two new companies, logistics firm Kühne+Nagel and telecommunications giant Swisscom are leaving the main composition. This move represents a small revolution and is described as the biggest change recorded in recent years on the Swiss stock market. SIX, the company that manages the Swiss stock exchange, had announced this change at the beginning of July. The ranking that determines promotions and relegations in the Olympus of the top 20 market values is based on two specific factors relating to the last twelve months: the average trading volume and the free-float capitalization, meaning the share of a company's capital that is freely tradable on the market. For positions 19 to 22, identified as the buffer zone, additional rules apply to avoid continuous changes caused by small shifts, thus offering members already present in the SMI an advantage over potential challengers.
### The impact on the pharmaceutical and healthcare sector The most obvious consequence of this recent stock market revision is that the pharmaceutical and healthcare sector is acquiring an even greater weight within the main Swiss index. In addition to the new entries represented by Galderma and Sandoz, Novartis, Roche, Lonza and Alcon are also part of the SMI. The total number of representatives of this branch therefore rises from four to six units. Analyzing the data in terms of capitalization, the shift is nevertheless less pronounced compared to the number of companies: the overall share of healthcare companies on the total SMI index rises in fact to about 40%, registering an increase compared to the previous 36%. As explained at the time of the announcement by Remo Rosenau, an expert at Helvetische Bank, the index does not represent the entire Swiss economy but shows the trend of the largest and most liquid listed companies and sectors. Although the index loses slightly in terms of explanatory capacity as a measure of the entire breadth of the national economy, this characteristic was also present previously, confirming that the SMI nevertheless remains an excellent benchmark index for the Swiss stock market, where certain branches naturally maintain a strong overall weight. ### Comparison with other markets and stock visibility
The prominent presence of individual sectors within the benchmark stock market indicator is not an exclusively Swiss peculiarity. Other well-known international indices also reflect their respective national economies only in part. For example, the Dow Jones Industrial Average illustrates the American economy even less representatively than the SMI does for the Swiss one. The entry of a given company into a well-known and closely watched index like the SMI is not merely a matter of corporate prestige; it concretely increases the visibility and attention paid to that stock by institutional and international investors. Since a vast number of investment funds and ETFs, meaning exchange-traded funds, faithfully replicate the index performance, inclusion can generate additional demand for the affected share, as these financial products are obliged to adjust their investment portfolios. As a rule, this process also leads to an increase in liquidity and trading activity on the market, making the stock potentially more attractive to further categories of investors. However, this effect does not automatically prove lasting over time, since a significant portion of the price movement is often anticipated by market operators even before the company's actual entry into the official benchmark index.
### Current composition and history of the index
Currently, excluding the changes just implemented, the SMI is composed in alphabetical order of ABB for electrical engineering, Alcon for ophthalmology, Amrize for industry, Geberit for sanitary products, Givaudan for flavors and fragrances, Holcim for building materials, Kühne+Nagel for logistics, Logitech for electronics, Lonza for pharmaceuticals, Nestlé for food, Novartis for pharmaceuticals, Partners Group for finance, Richemont for luxury goods, Roche for pharmaceuticals, Sika for specialty chemicals, Swiss Life for insurance, Swiss Re for reinsurance, Swisscom for telecommunications, UBS for banking services, and Zurich Insurance for insurance. If the ranking is instead drawn up on the basis of market capitalization, the giants Roche, Novartis, and Nestlé stand out. The Swiss Market Index was created almost four decades ago, exactly on June 30, 1988, starting from an initial level of 1,500 points. The lowest point in its history was touched on January 14, 1991, at 1,287.60 points, while over the years the value has multiplied by more than 9 times. Among the historical milestones are the 5,000 points reached in 1997, 10,000 in 2019, 12,000 in 2021, 13,000 in February 2025, and 14,000 points in February 2026, reaching an all-time high of 14,669.51 points on August 8 of last year. Today the index is hovering around 13,900 points. The best annual performance was in 1993 with a plus 40%, while the worst was recorded in 2008 with a minus 35%. Last year the index posted a plus 14.4%, while during 2026 the SMI has gained 4.9% so far. For economic history enthusiasts, in 1988 the first SMI included 22 companies, among which were Brown, Boveri & Cie, the Swiss People's Bank, Swiss Credit, Swiss Bank Corporation, Union Bank of Switzerland, Swissair, and Winterthur.

Those managing personal portfolios through indexed funds or ETFs must consider that the new sectoral weighting further shifts the center of gravity of the SMI towards the pharmaceutical and healthcare sector, which now accounts for approximately forty percent of the total capitalization. This means that risk exposure and the diversification of one's equity portfolio change structurally, marginally reducing the weight of traditional sectors such as logistics and telecommunications, previously represented by Kühne+Nagel and Swisscom. Institutional and private investors monitoring securities added to or removed from the index must carefully verify the liquidity and trading volumes of the individual securities involved, bearing in mind that price movements linked to the actual entry or exit from the main baskets often tend to be anticipated by the market in the weeks preceding the official implementation of the SIX resolution.

item.title: Security flaws in solar systems threaten the grid
item.description: The National Cybersecurity Testing Institute has detected over fifty vulnerabilities in eleven widely distributed photovoltaic products.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Over 50 vulnerabilities detected in photovoltaic systems - Seven out of eleven products present serious flaws - Risk of cyber attacks and remote manipulation - Minimum security requirements requested by politics
## Key facts - Testing agency: National Institute for Cybersecurity Testing - Tested products: 11 devices from 8 companies - Inverters analysed: 7 - Energy management systems: 4 - Critical vulnerabilities: 7 - Serious vulnerabilities: 6
Serious flaws in Swiss photovoltaic systems risk compromising their stability. The National Institute for Cybersecurity Testing examined eleven widely used products belonging to eight companies, identifying over fifty vulnerabilities in total. Among the examined devices are seven inverters, i.e., the electronic devices that convert direct current into alternating current, and four energy management systems. The investigation highlighted that seven of these issues were classified as critical and six as serious, while five of the eleven products presented at least one serious security flaw.
### Technical shortcomings identified
The technical analysis conducted by experts revealed alarming shortcomings. In practically all tested inverters, technicians managed to reduce the power fed into the grid to zero without any need for authentication. Additional vulnerabilities identified concerned preset passwords, unprotected maintenance accesses, and insufficient encryption that exposes components to unauthorized intrusions. Nevertheless, experts found no indications of intentionally inserted backdoors, understood as hidden methods to bypass normal authentication and security systems.
The main threat stems from the high level of interconnection of installations across Swiss territory. Many devices are linked to manufacturers' cloud services to receive updates and manage telemetry. Six of the identified vulnerabilities would allow potential attackers to simultaneously manipulate thousands of devices from a centralized location, enormously amplifying the scope of the energy risk.
As explained by Tobias Castagna, testing expert at the institute, it is not only the severity of a vulnerability that makes it dangerous, but also its scope, since a single flaw in a central component can affect thousands of photovoltaic installations simultaneously. On very sunny days, the photovoltaic sector temporarily covers more than half of Switzerland's current electricity consumption, making the grid particularly exposed to sudden fluctuations or induced blackouts. The general safety level of the analyzed products is not fundamentally worse than that of other Internet-connected devices available on the consumer or industrial market. What distinguishes these devices, however, is their systemic relevance for the national and cantonal electricity grid. A large‑scale cyber attack could theoretically compromise the stability of power supply, creating immediate imbalances between distributed generation and the country’s total energy demand.
### Risk scenario and market reaction
The concentration of thousands of plants linked to the same manufacturers’ cloud platforms represents a systemic vulnerability point. When a software update or remote connection is compromised, the domino effect can spread nationwide. Fortunately, in most of the cases examined, manufacturers have responded quickly after the vulnerabilities were reported by technicians, releasing corrective patches or modifying access protocols.
From the perspective of critical‑infrastructure protection, the situation highlights the need to rethink the cyber‑security perimeter—not only around large hydroelectric or nuclear plants, but also toward the myriad of small residential and commercial photovoltaic installations distributed across the territory. Those who manage a photovoltaic installation today depend on global components whose cybersecurity was traditionally not considered a parameter of stability for the Swiss electricity grid. The growing digitalization of the energy transition therefore imposes a radical shift in technological‑risk management on the part of installers, manufacturers, and grid operators.

Faced with the critical issues that emerged from cybersecurity tests, the institute recommends the immediate adoption of concrete preventive measures for all owners of photovoltaic systems and for operators in the sector. Practical indications include the strict use of individual access credentials, the strengthening of remote access and the physical or logical separation of photovoltaic systems from the rest of the company or home network. Manufacturers are also encouraged to integrate advanced security standards already in development and implement digital authentication for any software updates.
### Regulatory requests and future prospects
Institutionally, the institute calls on policy and federal authorities to introduce mandatory minimum requirements for all devices placed on the Swiss market. The Raiffeisen barometer, produced in collaboration with the Zurich University of Applied Sciences (ZHAW), indicates that the Swiss pension system has seen further improvement. The data show that the economic conditions of the pension systems have reached all-time highs, with a value of 725 points out of a maximum of 1000. This figure represents an increase of 28 points compared to the previous year and a significant jump when compared to the 587 points recorded in the first edition in 2018.
### The drivers of pension growth According to Jürg Portmann, co-head of the Risk & Insurance institute at ZHAW, this result is the product of two main factors: the excellent financial health of pension funds and a greater propensity for saving among the population. The improvement overall affects all three pillars of Swiss social security. Tashi Gumbatshang, an executive at Raiffeisen, confirmed that the current level is the highest ever recorded since the research began.
Despite the positive trend of the numbers, the analysis based on a survey conducted among over 1000 people between the ages of 18 and 65 reveals some critical issues. The main concern relates to the first pillar: 39% of respondents fear that the AVS will not be able to cover its expenses in the long term. This data highlights a contrast between the current solidity of the system and the perception of future instability regarding basic social security. ## Supplementary pension analysis The analysis of the barometer shows a clear change in personal saving habits. The share of people using a 3a pillar to supplement their old age has reached 79%, setting a new record. This trend indicates a greater awareness of the need to integrate the annuities of the first two pillars to maintain the standard of living after retirement.
### The Impact of New Deposit Rules An element of great interest for residents in Switzerland is the introduction, scheduled for the beginning of 2026, of the possibility of filling the contribution gaps in segment 3a afterwards. Jürg Portmann suggests that this novelty may provide a further boost to private saving. However, the current data show a gap between knowledge of the standard and its practical application: while 63% of the sample knows the new rule, only 5% actually made a supplementary payment.

## In brief - Ated calls for permanent digital bodies in Ticino - A cantonal Cyber Security Commission has been proposed - Objective: unite institutional, academic, and private expertise
## Key facts - Association: Ated - Professionals represented: 7,000 - Request recipients: State Chancellery and Norman Gobbi - Reference model: Digital Switzerland Advisory Committee
The Ticino umbrella association Ated, which brings together around 7,000 professionals active in the Tech, ICT, and Digital sectors, has submitted an official request to the State Chancellery and State Councillor Norman Gobbi. The initiative aims to establish two permanent bodies: an Advisory Group for the Canton's digital transformation and a Cantonal Cyber Security Commission. The request was presented during a meeting at Castelgrande with a delegation from the Grand Council, with the intent of bringing the debate directly into parliamentary venues. According to Ated President Luca Mauriello, the current management of digital affairs, characterized by only sporadic discussions, is no longer adequate due to the extreme speed at which technology evolves.
### Governance for digital transformation The model proposed for the advisory group is directly inspired by the Digital Switzerland Advisory Committee, active within the Federal Chancellery. The idea is to create a regular discussion platform that brings together various components of the region: the Canton, municipalities, the economic world, the ICT sector, the USI and SUPSI universities, educational institutions, and civil society. The function of this body would be advisory and proactive, allowing digital strategies to be harmonized transversally. At the same time, the Cyber Security Commission, inspired by the work of the Federal Office for Cybersecurity, would focus on networking authorities, critical infrastructure, and businesses, concentrating in particular on prevention and the capacity for a coordinated response against cyberattacks, an issue of growing urgency for the security of the entire Swiss economic and institutional system. Ated's initiative raises significant issues regarding the institutional governance of digitalization at the cantonal level. The invitation launched by President Mauriello to the members of the Ticino Parliament is to overcome party affiliations, arguing that the digital strategy must be understood as a unified vision for Ticino, devoid of right, center, or left connotations. The request for institutional stability clashes with political cycles, given that standing committees are usually established by the end of the election year. However, the association urges not to wait until 2027, reiterating that technology does not follow the cycles of legislatures. This divergence between the timescales of politics and those of technological innovation is a challenge common to many Swiss cantons, where the need for long-term planning must be reconciled with democratic decision-making processes.
### Skills distributed across the territory A central point of the proposal is the enhancement of the skills already present in the Canton. Ated emphasizes that there is no need to create new oversized bodies or recruit external figures, as the know-how is already widely distributed among institutions, local businesses, universities, and industry professionals. The stated goal is therefore not to claim positions within such bodies, but to foster institutional openness that allows existing skills to be systematically brought to the same table. item.title: National Council approves agreement with Mercosur
item.description: Green light from the National Council to the commercial agreement with Mercosur. 517 million for agriculture and 25 million against deforestation.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - The National Council approves the Mercosur agreement with 118 votes in favor. - 517 million allocated for agriculture in the 2028-2033 period. - An additional 25 million planned for the fight against deforestation. - The dossier returns to the States for a divergence on environmental credits.
## Key facts - Votes in favor: 118 - Votes against: 66 - Abstentions: 10 - Agricultural allocation period: 2028-2033 - Agriculture amount: 517 million francs - Deforestation funds: 25 million francs
The National Council has approved, at the end of an intense parliamentary debate, the free trade agreement between Switzerland and the Mercosur bloc, which includes Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay, and Uruguay. The vote recorded 118 votes in favor, 66 against, and 10 abstentions, thus overcoming the initial rejection expressed by the Chamber in June. The dossier must now return to the Council of States for a review, due to a divergence that emerged between the two Chambers regarding the funds allocated to international cooperation for environmental protection.
### A mediation between opposing interests The approval was possible thanks to overcoming the cross-vetoes that had previously blocked the agreement. On one hand, the compromise satisfied the demands of the agricultural sector, providing for an allocation of 517 million francs for the 2028-2033 period. Of this figure, 480 million are intended for investment credits, while 37 million will be used for the promotion of sales and agricultural exports. On the other hand, to address the concerns raised by circles sensitive to nature protection, the National Council decided to increase the resources allocated to international cooperation aimed at combating deforestation by 25 million francs, with particular attention to the Amazon. This decision differs from the position adopted on Monday by the 'senators', making a new parliamentary passage scheduled for tomorrow necessary. During the debate, the left attempted unsuccessfully to refer the dossier back to the Federal Council for a new consultation, arguing that the aid package for agriculture represents a strategy to obtain the consensus of producers without adequately addressing the critical issues related to human rights and the global climate crisis. The parliamentary debate highlighted how the Mercosur agreement is perceived by the center-right, including the Liberal Greens, as a strategic necessity for the Swiss export economy. In a historical period characterized by strong geopolitical tensions and growing fragmentation of international markets, with the consequent threat of increased tariffs, Switzerland is seeking to diversify its commercial outlets to reduce dependence on the European and US markets. Federal Councilor Guy Parmelin emphasized that the agreement is strategic, warning that the European Union has already provisionally implemented its own free trade agreement with the South American bloc as of the beginning of May. Every day of delay, according to the Federal Department of Economic Affairs, entails a loss of market share for Swiss companies competing with European partners.
### Economic impacts and market prospects Mercosur represents a pool of 270 million consumers, with an estimated annual value for Swiss exports between 3 and 4 billion francs. The agreement, once definitively ratified, would allow national companies to benefit from a tariff reduction of 155 million francs each year. These figures illustrate the scale of the economic opportunity that the Government intends to seize to support the competitiveness of the national industrial sector. However, the ratification process remains conditioned by significant political variables. Corina Gredig, representing the Liberal Greens, highlighted how the agreement is susceptible to a popular referendum, the success of which could depend strictly on the guarantees provided regarding the deforestation of the Amazon. The inquiries cited during parliamentary proceedings suggest that, in the absence of stringent environmental measures, the majority of the Swiss population could oppose the agreement during a popular consultation. Precisely to mitigate this risk, the majority of Parliament decided to strengthen environmental commitments, integrating into the Federal Council's mandate the obligation to develop effective programs against deforestation and to constantly monitor the effects of the agreement on various economic sectors, periodically involving the competent committees to evaluate the progress of international cooperation and the sustainability of the production chains involved in trade with South American countries.

item.description: IFPDT and privatim's new official guide on digital surveillance via cameras, infrared and radar in healthcare facilities has been published.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - New guide on digital surveillance - Published by FDPIC and privatim - Hospital monitoring under scrutiny - Protection of data for cared-for individuals
## Key facts - Date: September 16, 2026 - Authorities: FDPIC and privatim - Sector: Hospitals and social-medical facilities - Technologies: Cameras, infrared sensors, and radar
The use of cameras, infrared sensors, or radar to monitor cared-for individuals in hospitals or similar facilities is becoming increasingly relevant in today's healthcare landscape. On September 16, 2026, the FDPIC and privatim published an official guide aimed at illustrating fundamental data protection issues and raising awareness among facilities intending to use this type of technological surveillance. Digital surveillance of cared-for individuals in hospitals, social-medical facilities, and other care institutions can take various operational forms. It may involve direct surveillance, which provides real-time image transmission to healthcare staff. Alternatively, it can be indirect surveillance, based on converting images into pictograms that indicate the real-time position of the person within the room. There is also a situational form, characterized by sending a signal or pictogram to the staff only in the event of a predefined occurrence, such as a fall from a bed. Whether based on optical cameras, infrared sensors, or radar, this form of surveillance involves high-intensity data processing. Such monitoring directly intervenes in the private, and sometimes even intimate, sphere of the cared-for individuals, who are often in situations of particular vulnerability.
### Common regulatory principles for surveillance Regardless of the type of surveillance and the specific technology used by the facilities, the principles and rules to be respected remain the same throughout the territory. First and foremost, surveillance must be lawful. Regarding public facilities, such as cantonal hospitals and nursing homes with a public mandate, the principle of legality strictly applies. This means that surveillance must be provided for, more or less directly, by cantonal law. For private facilities, such as clinics without a public mandate, lawfulness fundamentally depends on compliance with the principles enshrined in the Federal Act on Data Protection. The consent of the data subjects, although desirable where possible, is neither necessary nor sufficient to justify surveillance, and this applies to both public and private facilities. Informing the cared-for individual, on the other hand, plays an essential role in the process: every patient must be clearly informed regarding the objective of the surveillance and its specific implications. The purposes for which digital surveillance is implemented must be strictly defined and oriented exclusively toward the interest of the care recipient, such as improving their overall safety. Purely logistical reasons, such as simply verifying that staff have made a bed, are not considered sufficient to justify such invasive data processing. Furthermore, digital surveillance must always be proportional to the stated purpose and must represent a subsidiary measure compared to other less invasive solutions. If the primary objective is to prevent nighttime falls, alternative measures, such as the use of bed rails, must be considered as a priority. The technological solution adopted must have the least possible impact on the life of the care recipient. Consequently, indirect or situational surveillance, meaning activated only in the event of an incident, should be favored over continuous real-time monitoring, sending staff only the strictly necessary data and preserving privacy outside of critical situations.
### Security and Organizational Transparency Requirements A further central aspect concerns compliance with the principles of privacy by design and data security. This implies the design and adoption of technical solutions that best guarantee the protection and security of the collected information, taking due account of all relevant factors of the operational context. These include effectiveness regarding the pursued purpose, management of associated risks, availability of valid alternatives, as well as the organizational and financial constraints of the institution. When a healthcare facility evaluates the adoption of a digital surveillance system, it is required to follow a rigorous path: precisely define the pursued objectives, fully understand the implications of the chosen solution and its relative configuration options to avoid unnecessary data processing, document all choices made also through dedicated risk analyses, keep technical and organizational documentation constantly updated, regularly evaluate and control the system in use to certify its adequacy over time, and finally adequately train staff to ensure fully compliant and responsible use of such technological tools within the facility.
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). ### Operations and controls for healthcare facilities Healthcare institutions that intend to introduce or revise monitoring systems based on cameras, infrared sensors, or radars must establish a structured internal roadmap. The first operational step consists of drafting formal documentation that justifies the adoption of the technology in terms of necessity and proportionality. This preliminary phase must exclude the use of purely logistical or management motivations. Subsequently, an in-depth analysis of the risks related to privacy and the protection of the personal data of the people being cared for must be carried out. This analysis must consider the possibility of opting for less invasive solutions, such as situational surveillance systems or indirect surveillance via pictograms, which minimize the transmission of detailed images to healthcare personnel. Regulatory compliance also requires the verification of the reference legal framework, clearly distinguishing between the position of public facilities, bound by the principle of legality and cantonal law, and that of private clinics, which must strictly adhere to the dictates of the Federal Act on Data Protection.
The practical implementation phase cannot disregard constant monitoring activity and a targeted training plan aimed at all healthcare workers involved in the use of the devices. Personnel must be trained not only on the correct technical operation of the equipment, but also on the limits imposed by regulations regarding high-intensity data processing. ## In brief - Situation worsened in 2025 and the first half of 2026 - Population growth and rents are closely linked - Growth in the housing stock expected no earlier than 2027
## Key facts - Date: September 16, 2026 - Office: Federal Housing Office - Population growth 1990-2025: 36.9% - New homes on pre-existing buildings in 2025: 18% - Available building zones in 2022: 6.9%
The latest update from the online housing market monitoring of the Federal Housing Office shows that the situation in Switzerland further deteriorated in 2025 and the first half of 2026. Individuals with medium or low purchasing power looking for housing are particularly affected. The analysis also examines the relationship between immigration and the housing market in detail: it turns out that, in addition to demographic trends, income and housing supply also influence rent trends. Tensions in the Swiss housing market continue to rise. The situation remains particularly critical for households with low purchasing power, as well as in the metropolitan area of Zurich, Central Switzerland, and several mountain regions. One of the reasons is that too little is being built to keep pace with the increasing number of households. The increase in households is also linked to population growth. Between 1990 and 2025, the latter actually increased by 36.9%: 15.0 percentage points are attributable to the Swiss population, while 21.9 percentage points to the foreign population. Demographic growth increases the demand for housing, which also affects rent trends. However, income also plays an important role: if households can spend more on a house or an apartment, price pressure increases, especially if supply is limited. According to the analysis, in the long term, the effect of income on rents is almost equal to that of population growth. Two other factors are also decisive: the actual increase in the number of dwellings and the ability of supply to keep pace with demand. In 2025, about 18% of new homes were built in place of pre-existing buildings, thus limiting the net increase in the housing stock. Building land is also increasingly scarce: between 2012 and 2022 in the analyzed regions, the percentage of still available building zones fell from 9.9% to 6.9%. ### Demographic and territorial details The report highlights how pressure is concentrated in specific areas of the federal territory, creating strong regional disparities and putting pressure on the budgets of households looking for housing solutions suited to their economic possibilities. Foreign households more frequently looking for a home. The analysis also shows that foreign households, meaning those in which no one holds Swiss citizenship, are more mobile than Swiss ones. They account for about 21% of the total, but 39% of those that move. Ceteris paribus, they occupy about a quarter less living space per capita than Swiss households. In 2025, they averaged 2.08 people, slightly fewer than other households. Foreign households depend to a greater extent on the rental market: only 12% live in an owner-occupied home, compared to 42% of Swiss ones. Given that they move more often and on average enter into shorter-term contracts, they benefit less from the generally lower rents of older contracts. In relation to income, their rental expenses therefore tend to be higher. ### Impact on contracts and housing expenditure The analysis of residential mobility highlights particular dynamics related to the demographic composition of the country. Those who move more frequently inevitably face less favorable market conditions, having to sign new contracts subject to the most recent price increases, while those who have occupied the same dwelling for many years manage to benefit from conditions of greater economic stability and historically lower rents compared to the current average recorded in the various Swiss regions.

item.title: Moutier: over 400 pensioners receive a double AVS pension by mistake
item.description: A misunderstanding between Bern and Jura led to a double payment of AVS annuities, creating potential financial hardship for pensioners.
item.content:encoded:
## In breve - **Pensionati di Moutier (JU)**: oltre 400 hanno ricevuto la rendita AVS due volte a gennaio. - Malinteso tra cantoni: Berna e Giura hanno entrambi versato le rendite, ma garantiscono di aver agito correttamente. - Rimborso: la grande maggioranza delle rendite è stata rimborsata, ma restano in sospeso quasi 34.000 CHF per 18 beneficiari.
## Fatti chiave - Cantoni: Berna e Giura. - Beneficiari: oltre 400 pensionati di Moutier. - Importo: quasi 34.000 CHF in sospeso per 18 beneficiari. - Istituzioni: Cassa di compensazione del Canton Berna (CCB), Istituto cantonale giurassiano delle assicurazioni sociali (ECAS Jura).
A Moutier, nel Canton Giura, si è verificato un malinteso che ha portato oltre 400 pensionati a ricevere la loro rendita AVS due volte nel mese di gennaio. I cantoni di Berna e Giura, coinvolti nel trasferimento cantonale della città, hanno entrambi proceduto al versamento delle rendite, ma assicurano di aver agito correttamente secondo il diritto vigente.
Secondo l'esecutivo bernese, la Cassa di compensazione del Canton Berna (CCB) non ha commesso errori. La CCB è rimasta responsabile del versamento delle rendite fino al cambiamento formale delle competenze, che non era ancora avvenuto. L'ECAS Jura, l'istituto cantonale giurassiano, avrebbe dovuto richiedere attivamente i dossier delle rendite per assumere il versamento, ma non lo ha fatto formalmente.
L'ECAS Jura, contattato dall'agenzia Keystone-ATS, ha dichiarato che la ripresa del diritto alle prestazioni complementari dal 1° gennaio implicava anche la ripresa del versamento delle rendite. Il Fondo AVS ne era stato informato e aveva fornito gli importi necessari per garantire il pagamento delle rendite a partire da gennaio 2026.
Dopo questo malinteso, la maggior parte delle rendite è stata rimborsata, ma restano ancora in sospeso quasi 34.000 CHF per 18 beneficiari. Questi importi verranno dedotti dalle future rendite nel mese di dicembre. ## Practical Implications This episode highlights the complexity of administrative procedures and the need for clear communication between the institutions involved in the cantonal transfer of Moutier. The misunderstanding led to a double payment of AVS annuities, creating potential financial hardship for the pensioners involved.

item.title: Health insurance premiums Canton Glarus: bands, deductibles and reduction
item.description: In the Canton of Glarus, LAMal premiums vary by premium range and deductible; it is possible to obtain the cantonal reduction within three months of registration.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - LAMal mandatory for all residents, to be taken out within 3 months - Adult deductibles available: 300‑2500 CHF - Premium reduction is a cantonal subsidy, subject to eligibility
## Key facts Mandatory → yes Enrollment deadline → 3 months Deductibles available → 300/500/1000/1500/2000/2500 CHF Premium reduction → cantonal subsidy Premiums → per capita, vary by canton
In the Canton of Glarus the compulsory health insurance (LAMal, also known as KVG) follows national rules: all residents must take it out within three months of moving. Premiums are set at cantonal level, so they can differ from one canton to another, but the basic structure is common to the whole Confederation. 📊
Adult deductibles are set at six levels: 300, 500, 1 000, 1 500, 2 000 and 2 500 CHF. The insured chooses the deductible at the time of subscription; a higher deductible lowers the monthly premium but increases the amount of expenses to be covered in case of care. The premium is calculated per capita, i.e., it is not linked to salary contributions or income tax.
The Canton of Glarus also provides a subsidy for premium reduction, intended for families and individuals who meet specific income requirements. The reduction is not automatic: an application must be submitted to the cantonal health department, attaching documentation proving the financial situation. The procedure is open annually and decisions are communicated within a few weeks.
The Swiss tax system has three levels – federal, cantonal and communal – with specific multipliers for each canton. Although LAMal premiums are not subject to income tax, their amount affects the cost of living, especially in regions with higher premiums. In the broader context, AVS/AHV, LPP/BVG and VAT remain the main fiscal elements that residents have to manage together with the payment of insurance premiums.
### How the cantonal reduction works The Glarus health department assesses the application based on taxable income, number of dependents and the chosen deductible. If the reduction is granted, the benefit translates into a percentage reduction of the monthly premium, which can vary year by year depending on the cantonal budget. No salary contribution is required for LAMal, so the reduction directly impacts the household budget. ## Practical analysis The mechanism of reducing LAMal premiums in the Canton of Glarus has concrete repercussions both on household budgets and on the canton’s competitiveness compared to other Swiss regions. Before the subsidy was introduced, families had to bear the full premium, regardless of income. With the reduction, low‑income families see a decrease in their monthly cost, helping to contain the cost of living, a factor that also affects housing expenses and consumption.
From a fiscal perspective, the premium reduction does not directly affect the federal direct tax nor VAT, but it reduces discretionary household spending, leaving more room for the payment of other taxes such as cantonal and municipal ones. Moreover, the savings can be directed to investments in retirement products such as the third pillar (3a), or to voluntary contributions to the LPP/BVG, improving the pension position.
Another relevant aspect is the comparison with cantons that have introduced a cantonal minimum wage. Glarus does not have a federal minimum wage, but the reduction of LAMal premiums can act as an "indirect benefit" for lower‑paid workers, compensating for the absence of a minimum wage threshold.
### Hypothetical scenario Imagine a family with two adults and two children, an annual taxable income of CHF 80,000. Choosing a deductible of CHF 1,500, the average monthly premium per adult is about CHF 300 (value not yet specified). Without the reduction, the annual expense would be about CHF 7,200. With the cantonal subsidy, the reduction could fall to 20 % of the premium, saving roughly CHF 1,440 per year. This amount, if allocated to voluntary contributions to the LPP, would increase the future pension by a few hundred francs.
From a labour‑market perspective, the presence of a subsidy for LAMal premiums makes the canton more attractive to employees from other regions, especially those who consider the overall cost of living when choosing a work location. Moreover, companies benefit from a more stable workforce, as employees have fewer financial worries related to health‑coverage.
Finally, the transparency of the eligibility criteria, managed by the health department, ensures that the benefit is distributed fairly, avoiding discrimination and fostering social cohesion within the canton.

If the deadline has passed, contact your insurer to regularize the position. 2. Collect the documentation – Prepare to provide: certificate of residence, most recent tax return, certificate of family composition and copy of the LAMal insurance contract with the chosen deductible. 3. Access the cantonal portal – Visit the official website of the Glarus Health Department and select the "LAMal premium reduction request" section. Enter the required data and attach the documents in PDF format. 4. Fill in the form – Follow the step-by-step instructions; the form asks for information on taxable income, the number of dependents and the chosen deductible. If in doubt, use our health to compare the different deductible options. 5. Submit the question – After verifying the correctness of the data, submit the request. The health department will evaluate the practice within 2-3 weeks. 6. Receive confirmation – If approved, you will receive a written communication with the amount of the reduction and the effective date. Update your insurer with the new premium quota. 7. Monitor annual deadlines – The reduction is granted for a period of one year. Before the deadline, check if you need to resubmit

item.title: LAMal Glarus: deductibles, subsidy and model choice
item.description: In Glarus, LAMal insurance is mandatory within 3 months, with deductibles from CHF 300 to CHF 2,500 and possible cantonal reductions based on income and family composition.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Mandatory LAMal premiums for all residents - Deductibles available: 300‑2500 CHF - Cantonal reduction based on income and family composition - Choice between HMO, telmed and traditional models
## Key facts - Mandatory insurance: LAMal/KVG - Subscription deadline: 3 months after moving - Adult deductibles: 300‑2500 CHF - Premium reduction: cantonal subsidy not yet specified - Salary contributions: AVS/AHV 5.3 % employee, LPP 7‑18 % depending on age - Taxation: 3 levels (federal, cantonal, municipal)
In the Canton of Glarus, as in all Swiss cantons, mandatory health insurance (LAMal, also known as KVG) must be taken out within three months of the resident's arrival. It is a private per‑capita premium coverage, therefore it is not a tax nor a salary contribution. Premiums vary according to the canton, the chosen insurance model and the selected deductible. Available deductibles for adults are 300, 500, 1 000, 1 500, 2 000 and 2 500 CHF; a higher deductible reduces the annual premium but increases the amount the insured must pay in case of a medical visit.
Glarus offers several alternative models besides the traditional free‑choice model: HMO (Health Maintenance Organization) plans limit the provider network but have lower premiums, while telmed models allow remote consultations at reduced costs. The choice of model directly affects the monthly premium, but the canton does not publish precise figures for each option; interested parties must consult insurers for details.
The canton also provides a premium reduction mechanism, often referred to as a “subsidy”. This subsidy is granted to those who meet certain income and family composition requirements; the exact criteria are not specified in the source, so it is advisable to check the competent cantonal office website. The reduction is not automatic: beneficiaries must submit an application documenting their income, any other insurance coverage and the number of dependents.
In the broader Swiss fiscal context, LAMal premiums are added to federal, cantonal and municipal direct taxes, as well as VAT. Insured persons must include the premiums in their tax return, as they are deductible within limits set by the Federal Tax Administration (AFC/ESTV). Other mandatory salary‑related charges include AVS/AHV (5.3 % employee) and LPP contributions, which range from 7 % to 18 % depending on age. To explore the impact of premiums on the payslip, you can use our [salary calculator](nav:calculator). ### Practical impact on household budgets
The cost of LAMal premiums directly affects the household budget, especially for low‑middle income brackets. Since premiums are set at the cantonal level, Glarus is among the cantons with medium‑high premiums, but the presence of deductibles up to CHF 2,500 allows modulating the annual expense. A taxpayer who chooses the highest deductible pays less during the year, but must be ready to bear a larger share in case of hospitalization or specialist visit. This dynamic is particularly relevant for families with multiple members, as the deductible applies per person.
The cantonal subsidy, although not specified in the source, is generally calculated based on taxable income and the number of dependents. Those who benefit from a reduction see a concrete decrease in the net premium, improving the capacity to save or invest in other pension pillars, such as LPP/BVG or the third pillar. In terms of fiscal policy, the premium reduction can translate into a lower deductible burden in the tax return, thus affecting both the federal direct tax and the cantonal tax.
From the perspective of health coverage, choosing the HMO or telmed model can reduce premiums by up to about ten percent, but it entails restrictions in the choice of doctors and hospitals. This trade‑off is often evaluated in relation to the cost of living, which in Glarus is influenced by factors such as access to public services, the housing market and job availability. For those who wish to compare their cost of living with that of other cantons, our [cost of living](nav:cost-of-living) provides a detailed overview.
Finally, it is useful to remember that LAMal premiums are not subject to salary contributions, but fall under deductible expenses. This differentiates health insurance from other obligations such as AHV/AVS or LPP, which are deducted directly from salary. Therefore, financial planning must take both aspects into account: the fixed premium portion and possible cantonal reductions, as well as the mandatory salary contributions.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Come ottenere la riduzione dei premi in Glarona
1. **Verifica la scadenza**: entro tre mesi dal trasferimento in Svizzera, stipula una polizza LAMal. Scegli la franchigia più adatta al tuo profilo di spesa sanitaria. 2. Raccogli i documenti: certificato di reddito (ultimi tre mesi), attestato di composizione familiare, eventuale dichiarazione di altri assicurazioni sanitarie. Questi documenti serviranno per la domanda di sussidio. 3. Accedi al portale cantonale: visita il sito dell’ufficio cantonale competente per le assicurazioni sociali. Qui troverai il modulo di richiesta riduzione premi, spesso disponibile in formato PDF scaricabile. 4. Compila il modulo: indica il tuo reddito imponibile, il numero di persone a carico e la franchigia scelta. Seleziona il modello assicurativo (tradizionale, HMO o telmed) poiché influisce sulla valutazione del sussidio. 5. Invia la domanda: allega i documenti richiesti e invia il modulo entro la scadenza indicata (solitamente entro 30 giorni dalla stipula della polizza). La conferma di ricezione è inviata via email o posta. 6. Attendi la risposta: l’ufficio cantonale valuterà la tua domanda e ti comunicherà l’importo della riduzione, se concessa. In caso di esito negativo, è possibile presentare ricorso entro 30 giorni. 7. Aggiorna la tua polizza: una volta ottenuta la riduzione, il nuovo importo sarà applicato al prossimo pagamento annuale. Controlla regolarmente la tua busta paga per verificare l’integrazione dei premi LAMal e dei contributi AVS/AHV.
Questa procedura è valida per tutti i residenti in Glarona, indipendentemente dal fatto che siano dipendenti, autonomi o pensionati. Per chi ha più di un’assicurazione sanitaria, è consigliabile verificare eventuali sovrapposizioni prima di richiedere il sussidio.

Con queste informazioni, potrai ottimizzare la tua spesa sanitaria e garantire una copertura adeguata senza sorprese.
