item.description: Economic and public analysis between football and ice hockey in Switzerland: Super League revenues, hockey estimates and stadium appearances.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - The Swiss hockey championship starts on Tuesday evening - Football surpasses hockey in total revenue - The Super League generated 440 million francs - Hockey is estimated at around 300 million francs
- Discipline: Football and ice hockey in Switzerland - Season examined: 2024-2025 - Super League revenue: 440 million francs - Super League clubs: 12 - Hockey clubs: 14 - Estimated hockey revenue: Around 300 million francs - Average football spectators: 13,000 per match - Average hockey spectators: 7,500 per match - Total football spectators: Around 2.7 million - Total hockey spectators: Around 2.7 million - Hockey matches: 364 - Football matches: 228
The Swiss ice hockey championship officially kicks off on Tuesday evening, a sport that sparks great passion in Switzerland but has to contend with the competition of football, a discipline that has won over a few more fans in recent years. The radio broadcast SEIDISERA compared the two sports, hockey and football, analyzing financial and audience data. In terms of revenue, football outperforms hockey. The Swiss Football League published data for the 2024-2025 season, in which the twelve Super League clubs generated 440 million francs in turnover. For hockey, not all financial data from the clubs is available, but an estimate can be made taking into account that there are fourteen participating clubs: this brings the direct turnover to around 300 million francs.
### Revenue analysis and economic differences between clubs
The economic differences between the two disciplines do not stop solely at the total turnover generated during the sporting year. For a football team in Switzerland, the revenue item linked to the sale of players is of fundamental importance, a commercial and market operation that allows football clubs to cash in a few million francs even from individual transfers. This economic dynamic is not a reality for hockey teams, as explained by Marzio Minoli, RSI economic journalist. In the case of ice hockey, in fact, even if a player were to move to the National Hockey League (NHL), and therefore to the United States or Canada, the former Swiss team would only receive a meager sum as compensation or training reward, a far cry from the capital gains recorded in national professional football. On the front of public attendance and stadiums, economic and statistical analysis offers insights of great interest to understand the bond between fans and their respective sports disciplines within the Swiss national context. In the football championship, the recorded average was 13,000 people per match, while in ice hockey the average stands at 7,500 spectators per game. Despite the difference in the average per single event, during the examined season the overall total of spectators was practically equal, reaching 2.7 million attendances for both football and hockey. However, this tie in total audience numbers must be read in light of the competition calendar: ice hockey in the season under review played as many as 364 matches, compared to the 228 matches played in the football championship. ### The loyalty factor and the occupancy rate of the rinks Swiss ice hockey shows particularly surprising and noteworthy numbers in terms of fan loyalty to their beloved team. It is a sports discipline that manages to fill the rinks consistently, recording an average 90% occupancy of available seats in the stands. In certain arenas in Switzerland, it even reaches 100% occupancy of maximum capacity, as happens in Fribourg. This means that, despite a lower number of spectators in absolute terms compared to football, the rinks and ice arenas are consistently full. To make a direct comparison with football stadiums, the latter instead record an average occupancy of 65% of available seats. A further distinguishing element emerges from a study by the University of Lausanne, which highlights how Swiss hockey represents a true powerhouse at the international level: the Swiss national team is currently number one in the International Ice Hockey Federation ranking and the Swiss championship turns out to be the second most popular tournament in the world, positioning itself immediately behind the North American NHL.
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). A determining aspect that profoundly differentiates the two sporting worlds concerns the sense of territorial belonging and the perceived national identity of fans in the stands. The hockey fan finds a strong national and local identity in their favorite team. This bond is also favored by the composition of the rosters: the majority of players fielded in hockey teams are of Swiss nationality, as regulations establish that foreign players who can take the field are limited to a maximum of six units. Conversely, in the football championship, the percentage of foreign players in the squads can reach up to 60%. The situation takes on even more marked contours when analyzing the geographical origin of athletes in club teams.
### Connection with the territory and economic perspectives
Many ice hockey teams in Switzerland regularly feature players coming directly from the region where the club is based. Taking the realities of Lugano and Ambrì Piotta as examples, both can boast the presence of several Ticinese players in starting roles, while by comparison FC Lugano does not have a single one in its squad. In summary, as highlighted by the economic and sports analysis, football turns out to be more powerful from a strictly economic standpoint and enjoys greater international appeal, but hockey proves decidedly more popular and rooted thanks to its visceral bond with the territory and local communities. Cooperation between the police and the army proved effective during the joint exercise called FIDES 26, which took place from Saturday until today in the Canton of Bern. Security bodies provide mutual support in exceptional situations, confirming how enhanced collaboration concretely contributes to the region's security. The event was jointly organized by the Cantonal Security Department, the Cantonal Police, and Territorial Division 1 of the Army, requiring almost two years of intense planning before its actual implementation in the field.

Field activities focused in particular on the protection of critical infrastructure and the targeted intervention of special units, testing the resilience of security mechanisms in the face of complex and prolonged events.
### Evaluation and analysis of weak points Initial lessons learned by those in charge show that cooperation between the cantonal police and Territorial Division 1 worked well overall regarding the assignment of tasks, the coordination of intervention forces, and the exchange of information. Data on overnight stays recorded in August indicate a slow normalization of tourist demand in the country. This is Switzerland Tourism's official reaction to the information published in the afternoon by the Federal Statistical Office, which specifically certifies a 2.1% decrease in overnight stays compared to the same period of the previous year. The tourism promotion organization summarizes that the need for security and stability, together with repeated heatwaves, led to an increase in demand for summer holidays—between the months of June and August—in the Confederation by Swiss, European, and American guests. This flow largely compensated for the sharp drop in visitors coming from Gulf countries and Asia. The overall picture emerging from these surveys is therefore decidedly varied.
### Analysis of tourist flows Switzerland Tourism experts highlight how the situation differs according to the various geographical regions of the national territory. While Graubünden or Zermatt clearly benefited from the combination of a scorching summer and a particular focus on the domestic market, destinations like Geneva or Interlaken were heavily affected by the absence of guests belonging to the Arab and Asian middle class. Supporting the summer season was the phenomenon of Nahweh, meaning the trend of preferring nearby destinations, which was clearly observable in these months although not uniformly across the entire country. ## Key facts - Tax levels: Federal direct tax (IFD), cantonal and municipal - Registration: Cantonal commercial register - Insurance: AHV/IV/EO, ALV, UVG and BVG
Starting a business in the Canton of Nidwalden requires precise planning that begins with choosing the legal form best suited to your entrepreneurial needs. The Swiss system, valid throughout the national territory, provides for mandatory steps that begin with registering the company in the cantonal commercial register. This requirement is not just a legal obligation, but represents the moment in which the economic entity acquires its legal personality, which is necessary to operate on the market with full validity towards third parties and authorities.
### The structure of the tax system The Swiss tax system operates on three distinct levels: the federal direct tax (IFD), managed by the Federal Tax Administration (FTA), cantonal taxes, and municipal taxes. Each canton sets its own tax rates and the relative tax multiplier for the municipalities. It is essential to understand that, although there is a federal framework, the operational management of payments takes place at the cantonal administrations competent for the territory. Companies must carefully monitor the overall tax burden, considering that cantonal and municipal taxes vary significantly between one jurisdiction and another, directly influencing the competitiveness of the business started in the territory of Nidwalden. The practical analysis for those intending to open a business in Canton Nidwalden must focus on obligations related to personnel and social security. When a company hires employees, the Swiss social contributions system comes into play, managed at the national level to ensure uniform coverage. OASI, IV, and EO contributions amount to a total of 10,6% of the salary, divided equally between employer and employee, each paying 5,3%. Added to this is unemployment insurance (UI), calculated at a rate of 1,1% up to the annual ceiling established by federal regulations.
### Risk Management and Social Security In addition to social contributions, companies must integrate accident insurance (UVG), with premiums varying between 0,7% and 1,5% depending on the sector of activity. Occupational pension provision (BVG) represents another mandatory pillar for employees, with contribution rates that increase progressively based on the worker's age, starting from 7% for the 25-34 age bracket up to 18% for those over 55. The retail giant Migros has announced a new reorganisation of its internal structures, introducing important changes at managerial and corporate level. At the center of the reorganization is the company Migros Online, which in the future will operate even more autonomously than in the past. As communicated by the Migros Federation of Cooperatives, the company will be managed as an independent entity within a completely new sector of activity called Online Retail. This new sector effectively replaces the current Non-Food sector within the Swiss group's organisation. The other three strategic branches that make up the group, namely Food Retail, Health and Financial Services, will not undergo any structural changes and will continue to operate according to the current approach. The decision reflects the management's willingness to adapt operating models to the changing conditions of the digital market and the consumption habits of Swiss customers.
### The details The profound structural reorganization announced by the large retail group inevitably involves important changes at the top of the company and within the supervisory bodies. Following this reshuffle, Matthias Wunderlin, who has so far served as chairman of the board of directors of Migros Online, will leave his post along with two other members of the supervisory body. The departure of these executives paves the way for a new phase of governance for the company active in food electronic commerce. The chairmanship of the board of directors is in fact entrusted to Florian Teuteberg, who already holds the role of CEO and co-founder of Digitec Galaxus and who was already part of the board of directors of Migros Online since 2018. This appointment represents a clear signal of the integration of digital skills within the Swiss group's decision-making leadership.
### The new members of the board of directors
Alongside the appointment of the new president, Migros Online's supervisory body is enriched with two new faces that bring a wealth of leading technical and commercial skills to the company. ### Underlying political guidelines During the 2023-2027 legislative term, the Federal Council's action is based on four fundamental strategic directions. The first direction establishes that Switzerland must ensure its prosperity in a sustainable manner, fully seizing the opportunities offered by digital technology. The second direction promotes national and intergenerational cohesion within the country. The third direction guarantees security, actively promotes peace, and ensures coherent and reliable action at the international level. These four pillars are accompanied by twenty-five specific thematic objectives valid for the entire duration of the legislative term, regularly monitored through official publications that associate individual measures with different thematic areas. ### Economic and financial priorities for 2027 During 2027, the Federal Council's agenda will see the adoption of major legislative and financial acts intended to influence Switzerland's economic framework. These measures will directly affect the future balances of the Swiss welfare system and the management of social benefits at the federal level.
